newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia minister sets sights on presidency.
newsitem.headline: Colombia minister sets sights on presidency.

text.p: Horacio Serpa, Colombia's Interior Minister and the strongman of President Ernesto Samper's administration, has resigned to prepare a bid for the presidency, government sources said Tuesday.

The Radionet radio network reported Samper had accepted the resignation of his right-hand man around midday (1700 GMT) but there was no immediate official confirmation. The move comes less than a week before the May 31 deadline by which prospective candidates must step down from public office -- exactly a year before elections to choose Samper's successor.

Serpa, 53, a ruling Liberal Party member, has been at the helm of the Interior Ministry since Samper took office in August 1994. He earned himself a reputation as the president's staunchest ally in the cabinet, leading political analysts to suggest that if Serpa were elected president he would pursue similar policies to those of the current administration.

Serpa, an able politician and a gifted public speaker, was in the frontline defending Samper against debilitating accusations that he financed his 1994 election campaign with drug money from the infamous Cali cartel.
Samper was cleared of wrongdoing in a congressional inquiry last year. But Serpa, one of the campaign organisers, is still under investigation on suspicion of knowingly accepting illicit donations.

In addition to rounding on Samper's opponents at home, Serpa has launched attacks against the president's fiercest international critic -- the United States. He recently dubbed U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette a "sick gringo" for what he claimed was the envoy's constant meddling in Colombia's internal affairs, especially relating to anti-drug policy.

Recent opinions polls show Serpa lagging behind the former chief prosecutor turned presidential candidate Alfonso Valdivieso, a thorn in the side of Samper's administration for his pursuit of political corruption.

But Valdivieso, also a Liberal, shunned his party's backing and announced he will run as an independent. Serpa, meanwhile, is likely to be able to count on the full political and financial support of the well-greased party machinery, which political analysts believe will greatly strengthen his hand as the presidential campaign gets into full swing.

The outgoing interior minister began his political career as mayor of the oil-production centre of Barrancabermeja in 1970 and has held numerous local and national government posts. He was one of the government negotiators during failed peace talks with leftist rebel groups in the early 1990s.
